Martin Sweeney was found at the victim’s suite at the residential hotel. The lamp came down with him and the bulb is still warm in its socket, unbroken. The El going over came at 8:30 PM, and the El was running to timetable and it covers the half hour exactly. That puts the killing in that half hour and no later.
The coroner puts death between 8:30 PM and 10:00 PM — two hours of nothing useful. One depressed fracture at the back of the skull. Death was not instant.
A bronze bookend is gone from the lobby of the Wyckoff. There is a clean square in the dust where it stood.
Carmela Marchetti puts Martin Sweeney at the third-floor walk-up on Ninth while the lesson was still going on overhead, which was 8:00 PM, and alive enough to argue about the weather.
Chandler Havemeyer was at the lobby of the Wyckoff at 8:30 PM and heard a heavy fall and a cry cut short from the direction of the victim’s suite at the residential hotel, just as the El went over.
Found at the victim’s suite at the residential hotel: A clipping about the failure of Vincenzo Grasso’s business, with Martin Sweeney’s name underlined twice in pencil.
Margaret Callahan says Vincenzo Grasso said Martin Sweeney had taken everything and would be made to feel it.
Found at the victim’s suite at the residential hotel: A promissory note for $4,000 signed by Gretchen Kreuzer, endorsed to Martin Sweeney, three months past due.
Margarethe Schilling says Martin Sweeney told Gretchen Kreuzer that Friday was the end of it, one way or the other.
Found at the garage on Eleventh Avenue: A subpoena naming Martin Sweeney before the grand jury, with Sterling Coffin’s name written in the margin.
Gretchen Kreuzer says Martin Sweeney said to Sterling Coffin that a man who testifies sleeps better.
Found at the third-floor walk-up on Ninth: A typed page of dates and sums in Martin Sweeney’s file, headed with Margarethe Schilling’s name.
James Mulcahy says Martin Sweeney told Margarethe Schilling that the story would run whether Margarethe Schilling liked it or not.
Vincenzo Grasso hired us. Vincenzo Grasso wants it known that Gretchen Kreuzer owed the victim money, and would rather we started there.
Carmela Marchetti on Gretchen Kreuzer: Gretchen Kreuzer’s registration card gives an address on a street that does not exist.
Chandler Havemeyer on Gretchen Kreuzer: Two signatures of Gretchen Kreuzer’s, a month apart, are in different hands.
Nora Hanrahan on Gretchen Kreuzer: Gretchen Kreuzer answers to the name a half-second late, every time.
A union card in Gretchen Kreuzer’s coat lining carries a different surname and a 1919 date.
A steamship ticket stub among Gretchen Kreuzer’s things, in the name of a man who died at Belleau Wood.
The name Gretchen Kreuzer was born with turns up on a desertion warrant from 1918. Gretchen Kreuzer has been hiding from the Army for eleven years and from nobody else.
The papers are forged and the reason is plain: Gretchen Kreuzer was put out of the country once already and does not mean to be put out twice.
Margaret Callahan on Nora Hanrahan: Nora Hanrahan had a key to the third-floor walk-up on Ninth that Nora Hanrahan had no business having.
Esther Feldman on Nora Hanrahan: The accounts at the third-floor walk-up on Ninth are in two hands, and the second hand only appears in the last column.
Gretchen Kreuzer on Nora Hanrahan: Somebody heard a drawer being worked at the third-floor walk-up on Ninth some time after 8:30 PM.
A carbon of a deposit slip at the third-floor walk-up on Ninth, made out in Nora Hanrahan’s hand to an account in another name.
Ledger pages at the third-floor walk-up on Ninth where the totals have been rubbed and written over.

The bank confirms the account: Nora Hanrahan has been taking two hundred a month for a year, and was at the third-floor walk-up on Ninth doing exactly that from 8:30 PM. It is theft, and it is not murder.
The books at the third-floor walk-up on Ninth settle it. Nora Hanrahan spent from 8:30 PM covering a hole in the accounts, which is why Nora Hanrahan would rather be suspected of anything else.
Nora Hanrahan on James Mulcahy: James Mulcahy and the victim were heard at the lobby of the Wyckoff, and one of them was doing all the talking.
Margarethe Schilling on James Mulcahy: James Mulcahy has come into money lately and has no visible way of having come into money.
Carmela Marchetti on James Mulcahy: The victim had been drawing cash in amounts that did not match anything in the accounts.
An envelope at the lobby of the Wyckoff with nothing in it, addressed in the victim’s hand to no one.
A photograph at the lobby of the Wyckoff, folded small, of something the victim would have paid to keep folded.
The victim’s bank book settles it: four payments, and James Mulcahy at the lobby of the Wyckoff from 7:00 PM collecting the fifth. It is extortion, and an extortionist wants the man alive.
The thing James Mulcahy was holding over the victim turns up, and it was worth more to James Mulcahy every month than once.
Vincenzo Grasso on Sterling Coffin: Sterling Coffin was carrying a parcel into the speakeasy under the hat shop and came out without it.
Nora Hanrahan on Sterling Coffin: There is a man who meets people at the speakeasy under the hat shop and nobody will say his name out loud.
Margarethe Schilling on Sterling Coffin: Sterling Coffin has been selling things that were never Sterling Coffin’s to sell.
Wrapping paper and a cut string at the speakeasy under the hat shop, and the shop it came from closed two years ago.
A pawn ticket at the speakeasy under the hat shop in a name that does not exist, made out at the hour in question.
